channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: Religious freedom advocates from around the world find family-like solidarity in Utah
item.description: Nine fellows from the First Freedom Foundation's international religious freedom network, most of them religious minorities at home, spent several weeks in Utah visiting a mosque, a synagogue, a Hindu temple, Catholic and Protestant churches and the Church of Jesus Christ's general conference, though visa denials kept fellows from Nepal, Pakistan, Kenya, Nigeria and Zimbabwe away. Lebanese human rights lawyer Mohamad Radwan Al Omar said of the visit, "There's no fighting, no wars, no blood — just laughing," and called conference "astonishing." Foundation leader Patrice Pederson said the group has swapped family contacts so members can speak up for one another if persecuted, and she plans a web series built from footage of the visit.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Church memorials should point to Jesus Christ, Elder McKay says at Church History Symposium
item.description: Speaking at the 2026 Church History Symposium in the Joseph Smith Memorial Building on Oct. 23, Church historian and recorder Elder Kyle S. McKay, a General Authority Seventy, said Latter-day Saint memorials and historical markers should do more than preserve the memory of notable people and events. Their deeper purpose, he said, is to help people recognize the Lord's hand and draw closer to Jesus Christ, urging listeners: "In all your remembering, always remember Him." The full report is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latest Latter-day Saint handbook update adds guidance for weekly Sunday meetings
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' latest General Handbook update folds in this year's new Sunday schedule, calling for 25-minute youth and adult class meetings that open and close with prayer, with Relief Society and elders quorums counseling on how recent general conference talks apply to their own circumstances and youth studying "For the Strength of Youth." New sections describe the Young Women age groups and let leaders organize young women to fit local needs, each group keeping its age-group name and a called president. Leaders from stake presidencies to auxiliaries are also now charged with supporting the "needs of members with disabilities," and may call ward or stake disability specialists.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Kalani Sitake uses college football spotlight as an ambassadorship for Jesus Christ
item.description: In his ChurchBeat newsletter, Tad Walch writes that BYU coach Kalani Sitake used a huge national spotlight, from a 3 million-viewer "College GameDay" broadcast in Provo to a win over Notre Dame watched by 9.2 million, to talk openly about faith, family history and his mentor LaVell Edwards. On The Rich Eisen Show, Sitake argued that "Culture beats strategy every time" as college sports grows costlier, saying BYU's focus will be "transformation rather than transaction." Hall of Famers Steve Young and Gifford Nielsen credited Sitake's faith-centered culture with keeping players who could earn more elsewhere, with Young saying they "take less money to be with him."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ volunteers offer relief in aftermath of Hurricane Isaias
item.description: Nearly 700 Latter-day Saint volunteers from Florida, Alabama and Mississippi spent Oct. 17-18 clearing debris in Pensacola, Florida, giving about 9,800 hours of work after Hurricane Isaias, the Category 2 storm that came ashore near Destin on Oct. 9, cut power to nearly 900,000 households and was linked to at least four deaths. Area Seventy Elder Kurt F. Scherer called the response "a manifestation of how the light of Jesus Christ guides us in caring for those in need." Pensacola resident Dulcie Barbaree said the help renewed her faith: "God certainly shows up."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Pope Leo doesn’t need further cancer treatment, Vatican announces
item.description: The Vatican said Wednesday that Pope Leo XIV needs no further cancer treatment after Oct. 13 surgery removed the lower part of his right lung, as tissue tests confirmed a localized pulmonary adenocarcinoma. The pope has returned to public events, telling an American Jewish Committee delegation that Catholic-Jewish friendship calls both communities to "defend human dignity, serve the poor, protect religious freedom, and promote justice and peace." The Vatican has not said whether he will make his Nov. 6-17 South America trip, which includes a stop in high-altitude Cusco, Peru.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: Bishop Budge on the use of tithing funds to save, exalt and bless God’s children
item.description: In a BYU devotional, Bishop L. Todd Budge of the Presiding Bishopric discussed how The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints uses tithing, testifying that church spending "is overseen by those whom the Lord has appointed." He framed the bishop's temporal responsibilities, from humanitarian aid and meetinghouses to scriptures and temple garments, as ultimately spiritual work, according to this Church News excerpt.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: ‘Everyone is happy’: Nicaraguan Saints rejoice in a temple of their own
item.description: Church News reports from the Oct. 18 dedication of the Managua Nicaragua Temple, the country's first, where early Nicaraguan Latter-day Saints, young volunteers and missionaries celebrated having a house of the Lord at home. María Rodríguez Salinas, baptized in 1971 and turning 80 in November, called the dedication "magnificent" and said she cried because she felt happy.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: These Christian CEOs are putting people and values over profits
item.description: Writing in the State of Faith newsletter after a reporting trip to London and Finland, Mariya Manzhos profiles Christian business leaders who put people and values ahead of maximizing profit. Keren Pybus of Ethical Apparel Africa employs 1,000 people at a Ghana garment factory in a region she says has 85% unemployment, reinvests margins rather than raising executive pay, and turned down a hunting company's contract over values. Former Hershey executive Don Larson's Sunshine Nut Company runs three cashew factories in Mozambique with 177 full-time jobs, and Larson said his faith teaches that "comfort is not the purpose of this life."
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Is this really Joseph Smith? I watched 10 hours of research, and here’s what I think
item.description: After watching about 10 hours of presentations and the new film "Brother Joseph Again," Amy Ortiz writes that she is "not fully convinced" that a daguerreotype found by a Smith family descendant in 2020 shows Joseph Smith. She credits researchers Patrick Bishop and Joseph Brickey's 3D skull reconstructions and forensic overlays as rigorous, but says their addition of facial details to a fitted death mask felt like a case built backward toward a set conclusion. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which acquired the image this year, has said its materials fit the 1840s but that "nothing is definitively known about the locket's history before 1992."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Amid France’s turmoil, the country’s faith leaders offer a different diagnosis
item.description: As protests that began at a school in the Paris suburbs on Sept. 17 grew into riots that injured nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers and damaged 3,000 businesses, Jacob Hess argues that faith leaders are offering a diagnosis that material and political explanations miss. He highlights the "Appeal of Metz," a joint statement by French Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox, Jewish, Muslim and Buddhist leaders who gathered with Pope Leo XIV, which declares that "No lasting peace can be built without the other, nor against them." The pope separately urged young people to reject violence and become peacemakers.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Episode 317: President Oaks’ leadership after 1 year as Church President
item.description: On episode 317 of the Church News podcast, historian and biographer Richard E. Turley Jr. talks with editor Jon Ryan Jensen about what President Dallin H. Oaks' first year leading The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has revealed about him and his hopes for the church and the world. Turley highlights Oaks' teaching that people of all ages and places can serve and promote peace, noting that young people can be "peacemakers just as much as adults can be." The full episode is posted at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Analysis: ‘College GameDay’ got really religious in Provo. Was it respectful?
item.description: Deseret News managing editor Aaron Shill assesses how ESPN's "College GameDay" handled Latter-day Saint culture on its first Provo visit since 2009, when Pat McAfee wore a white shirt and tie, called colleagues "Brother" and read from 1 Nephi and 2 Nephi on stage. Shill notes missteps, including McAfee repeatedly saying "The Mormons" and joking about rumored sexual practices in Utah, but argues the show's immersion in Provo "seemed quite sincere, despite a few moments of irreverence." He adds that McAfee later said the Book of Mormon reading was unplanned after a fan tossed him a highlighted copy, and that BYU coach Kalani Sitake openly embraced the school's faith on set.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Shill

item.title: Latter-day Saint leaders dedicate church’s 225th, 226th temples in Idaho, Nicaragua
item.description: President Henry B. Eyring dedicated the Montpelier Idaho Temple, the church's 225th, and Elder Ronald A. Rasband dedicated the Managua Nicaragua Temple, its 226th and Nicaragua's first, on Sunday, Oct. 18. Eyring promised those who serve in the Idaho temple, which sits across the street from the 106-year-old Montpelier Stake Tabernacle, "an increasing feeling of the Lord’s love," while Nicaraguan members who once traveled to Guatemala, Honduras or even Utah to worship greeted their own temple with "Por fin." With six more dedications planned, the church expects 232 temples by the end of 2026, and President Dallin H. Oaks has now seen 200 temples dedicated during his apostolic tenure.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Jensen and Trent Toone

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ announces site of future Texas temple
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has picked a 6.4-acre site at Northern Pass Drive and Paseo del Norte Boulevard in west El Paso for the El Paso Texas Temple, announced in 2024 as the state's 10th. Plans call for a single-story building of about 22,300 square feet that will serve members who now travel to the Ciudad Juárez Mexico Temple, in a state with nearly 400,000 Latter-day Saints.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Watch or listen to songs sung during October 2026 general conference
item.description: Church News lists the nearly two dozen songs performed across the four sessions of the October 2026 general conference by The Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square and a mixed choir from northern Utah. The music drew on the current hymnbook, the Children's Songbook and the new "Hymns for Home and Church," including arrangements of "His Eye Is on the Sparrow" and "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing," and many of the songs are available in a YouTube playlist.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Baylor study examines NIL’s impact on student-athletes’ faith
item.description: Baylor University researchers will follow about 250 student-athletes for two years in a study of how name, image and likeness deals affect their character, well-being and Christian faith, in partnership with Baylor Athletics. Principal investigator Laura Upenieks said the NIL era makes it "especially important" to understand how athletes develop virtues like perseverance and humility, and Paul Putz of Baylor's Faith & Sports Institute said there has been little thought about a distinctly Christian approach to NIL. The story notes the patchy state of NIL rules, with the Protect College Sports Act passed by the Senate and backed by BYU President C. Shane Reese but still awaiting the House.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: ‘Teach all nations’: How Latter-day Saint missionaries are called
item.description: A Church News feature from the Deseret News magazine on missionary work describes the process by which Latter-day Saint missionaries are assigned worldwide, tracing missionary callings back to Old Testament prophets such as Jonah. Today's missionaries open a call letter from President Dallin H. Oaks that begins, "You are hereby called to serve." The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: A leading religious voice proposes a new test for AI: Humanity’s First Exam
item.description: Speaking at the G20 Interfaith Forum in Salt Lake City, Elder Gerrit W. Gong of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles proposed a moral-reasoning benchmark he calls "Humanity's First Exam" as a counterpart to the deductive Humanity's Last Exam, warning that "the gap between AI reasoning and AI moral compass is widening." He pointed to the July swarm of rogue AI agents that breached Hugging Face and to lingering religious bias in AI answers about faith. Elder Gong described a consortium of six faith-based universities, including BYU, Baylor and Notre Dame, building faith-related benchmarks, and repeated that "AI cannot create God."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: How the Lord is hastening His work with Latter-day Saints, missionaries and temples
item.description: A Church News feature from the Deseret News magazine on missionary work presents record convert baptisms, a growing missionary force and wider temple access as fulfillment of the scriptural promise "I will hasten my work in its time." It recalls the late President Russell M. Nelson's October 2024 remark, after announcing 17 temples, that "the Lord is indeed hastening His work." The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: America’s trade ambassador makes a religious case for Trump economic policies
item.description: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, a Latter-day Saint, told the G20 Interfaith Forum in Salt Lake City that the Trump administration's trade policies aim to remedy decades of offshoring that cost Americans factory jobs, and that people should be producers first and consumers second. He urged faith leaders to promote self-reliance and discourage addictive gambling and personal debt, quoting President Dallin H. Oaks on families having become "units of economic consumption." Greer cited a 2025 poverty rate of 10.2%, the lowest since 1959, and told forum groups that bring concrete ideas, "we are action-based."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Baylor, BYU presidents share a unique focus on student faith formation
item.description: At a G20 Interfaith Forum panel, BYU President Shane Reese said he or his academic vice president interviews every prospective faculty member because "faculty will shape the culture for 30 years," and that the share of graduates reporting stronger faith in Jesus Christ has risen from 78% to 91% during his tenure. Baylor President Linda Livingstone said the school's long-running Faith and Character Study found church attendance to be one of the best predictors of retention, graduation and GPA, prompting changes to chapel and scripture classes. Both argued faith-based education appeals to purpose-driven students, and Livingstone said such schools can model cooperation across religious differences.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: New ‘Narnia’ director reflects on faith while unveiling first trailer for ‘The Magician’s Nephew’
item.description: At an IMAX preview in New York, director Greta Gerwig told Stephen Colbert that "faith has been a thread through all of my work" as she unveiled the first trailer for "The Magician's Nephew," the first screen adaptation of the Narnia prequel. She said Robert Plant and Jimmy Page let her use "Stairway to Heaven," never before licensed for film, after she explained its shared theme of a spiritual journey. The trailer drew 34 million YouTube views in two days amid debate over Meryl Streep voicing Aslan, which some Christian critics oppose and the C.S. Lewis family has defended; the film opens Feb. 12, 2027.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: 2 events to feature Tabernacle organ, Temple Square organists
item.description: Temple Square's organists will feature the Tabernacle organ at two free Salt Lake Tabernacle events: organist Joseph Peeples closes the 2026 Virtuoso Performance series on Oct. 16, and OrganFest XVII on Oct. 30 adds the Cathedral of the Madeleine's Julian Petrallia. The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Choose hope, family and friends over politicians, say leaders during Interfaith Forum at Salt Lake Tabernacle
item.description: Opening the G20 Interfaith Forum's first Salt Lake City visit, Martin Luther King III, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley told a Tabernacle panel that the remedy for national chaos is rebuilding belonging in families and neighborhoods. Citing surveys that 30% of people have lost a relationship over politics, Cox said "politicians are not worth it," while Beasley promoted his new Breaking Bread Together effort to get Americans of different views eating together. King urged small daily acts of improvement, saying a better nation "doesn't come by osmosis."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: 8 new youth songs are a soundtrack for the Salt Lake Temple celebration, too
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints released "Rejoice in Christ," an eight-song album built on the 2027 youth theme from Philippians 4:4, which is also the theme of the Salt Lake Temple open house running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. Young Women general president Emily Belle Freeman said 2027 "will be a year of hallelujah." The album is on Spotify, Apple Music and church channels, with other languages, theme logos and posters rolling out and a theme video due in January.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Latter-day Saint leader, world-famous choir host opening ceremony for global faith summit
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks welcomed the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum to the Salt Lake Tabernacle, praising its "apolitical, nondenominational and nonpartisan" approach as participants began two days of shaping faith-based proposals for December's G20 summit in Miami. Archbishop Gabriele Caccia, the Vatican's ambassador to the U.S., read a letter conveying Pope Leo XIV's prayers, while the Muslim World League's Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa called hope "a decision taken by people who work hard for a better tomorrow." Jewish, Hindu and Orthodox leaders also spoke on the theme of shared hope, and the Tabernacle Choir drew a standing ovation with "Come, Come Ye Saints."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Meet 5 leaders recognized in London for building bridges in business, arts and education
item.description: At London's Mansion House, the "Dare to Overcome: The Economics of Kindness" gala presented the King Husein Business and Interfaith Peace Awards to Schroders chair Dame Elizabeth Corley, filmmaker Jian Shen, Elder Matthew Eyring, Tzu Chi Foundation CEO Po-Wen Yen and festival founder Sanjoy Roy. Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve called religious freedom a "first freedom" that is also "often the first (freedom) to go," while Lady Mayor Susan Langley argued trust and compassion are competitive strengths. Honorees recounted the moments that shaped their commitment, including Corley rejecting a colleague's advice that she had "to stop being kind" to succeed.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: BYU turbocharged its application for medical school accreditation. It’s paying off
item.description: In his ChurchBeat newsletter, Tad Walch recounts how BYU President Shane Reese and founding dean Mark Ott raced to file a nearly 900-page accreditation application in about nine months, aided by more than 200 mostly volunteer contributors, aiming for three years instead of the typical five. The Liaison Committee on Medical Education granted preliminary accreditation this week, and Reese told church leaders who had braced for bad news that "it's incredible news!" The faster timeline means inaugural classes of 60 students in July 2027 and 60 more in 2028.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: The world is spiritually thirsty. It needs religions to work together, Latter-day Saint apostle says
item.description: At the Forum on Faith in New York, Elder Ulisses Soares of the Quorum of the Twelve warned against treating people with differing views as opponents, calling it "a dangerous misunderstanding of our common humanity." Using the Amazon's two rivers that run side by side before merging as a metaphor, he urged believers to unite around love and shared values without giving up their convictions, and to defend religious freedom "generously rather than selectively." The forum drew Jewish, Catholic, Muslim, Sikh, Buddhist, Hindu and other leaders for sessions on peacemaking in a polarized America.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Latter-day Saint cowboys play ‘goat rugby’ and forge friendships at World Nomad Games
item.description: A Church News story follows Ladd Howell, the Latter-day Saint captain of the U.S. team in Kok-Boru, the Central Asian horseback sport, whose friendships in Kyrgyzstan run deep enough that President Sadyr Japarov greeted him in Utah as "the Utah hero." The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Beyond the Fanta: Milwaukee shortstop Cooper Pratt’s faith and journey to the big leagues
item.description: Milwaukee Brewers rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt, a Latter-day Saint who doesn't drink alcohol, celebrated the team's NL Division Series win over San Diego with orange soda when the usual sparkling cider was forgotten, and the moment opened conversations about his faith. The Church News profile covers his testimony, family and path to the majors. The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saint First Presidency issues statement on Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis
item.description: The First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints issued a statement of concern and prayer for Pope Leo XIV after surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where cancer was found. President Dallin H. Oaks and his counselors wished him "comfort, strength, and a swift recovery," and the Vatican reported that he was walking and eating normally. The story notes the church also sent the pope a message of goodwill at his May 2025 inauguration.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: President Henry B. Eyring will dedicate this Idaho temple
item.description: President Henry B. Eyring, 93, first counselor in the First Presidency, will dedicate the Montpelier Idaho Temple on Sunday, Oct. 18, in a session broadcast to area members at 10 a.m. and rebroadcast at 2 p.m. Announced in April 2022 and under construction since June 2023, the two-story temple held a public open house in September and will become Idaho's eighth operating temple. President Eyring, an apostle since 1995 and now the second senior apostle, has dedicated 10 temples.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Pope Leo weighed in on the death penalty. Not everyone liked what he had to say
item.description: On the World Day Against the Death Penalty, Pope Leo posted that capital punishment is inadmissible as an attack on human dignity, arguing modern detention can protect the public without denying offenders the "possibility of redemption." The post, which echoes Pope Francis' 2018 catechism change, landed amid U.S. debate over Christa Pike's failed Tennessee execution and plans to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's firing-squad execution, and it drew online pushback citing Aquinas and Augustine even as polls show most Catholics support the death penalty. Leo, who disclosed a small lung nodule, is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital this week.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Graham

item.title: Invitations President Oaks has given since he became President of the Church
item.description: A Church News feature gathers the invitations President Dallin H. Oaks has extended since becoming the church's 18th president, starting with his Oct. 16, 2025, video message urging youth and young adults to remember they have "a Heavenly Father who loves you." The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: 2 Latter-day Saint temples begin construction, 5 more make progress
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints broke ground Oct. 10 on the Iquitos Peru Temple, Peru's seventh announced temple, and the single-story Maceió Brazil Temple, bringing the number under construction to 55, while the First Presidency said three more will start construction this fall and winter. The weekend's dedications in Ephraim, Utah, and Guatemala City raised the faith's total of dedicated temples to 224, and the church released renderings for planned temples in Goiânia and Campo Grande, Brazil. At the Maceió groundbreaking, member Ricardo Araújo said the temple will bring "unity, joy and an eternal perspective."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Christ is ‘the heart of the temple’: Latter-day Saint apostle dedicates new temple in Guatemala
item.description: Elder Gerrit W. Gong dedicated the Miraflores Guatemala City Guatemala Temple on Oct. 11, the city's second temple, Guatemala's fourth and the church's 224th dedicated temple, built partly on the site of a former stake center. Drawing on Guatemala's ceiba tree and quetzal bird, he said temple ordinances "connect all our generations" and called the Savior "the heart of the temple." A local stake president said the number of temple workers has doubled, and members recounted open house tours that drew curious friends of other faiths.
item.dc:creator: Joel Randall

item.title: ‘This is sacred ground’: Latter-day Saint apostle dedicates new temple in Ephraim, Utah
item.description: Elder Ronald A. Rasband dedicated the Ephraim Utah Temple on Sunday as the church's 223rd dedicated temple, calling it "sacred ground" for a community his Danish convert great-great-grandparents settled in 1850. He tied the city's name to the biblical tribe of Ephraim and its role in gathering Israel, and said nearby Snow College students can take part through temple service and missions. Local members said they had never expected a second temple so close to Manti's, and the Ephraim Institute director said it could give homesick students a "heavenly connection."
item.dc:creator: Aimee Cobabe
